title: SEER: Robust Time Series with Smart Patch Replacement
one_liner: Replace broken time series patches with strong summary markers before forecasting, so corrupted data does not ruin predictions.
lead: Time series forecasting reads past data to predict the future. But real data is messy: measurements go missing, equipment drifts, rare events spike, or noise creeps in. A single bad chunk of measurements can flip the whole forecast. This paper detects broken chunks (called patches) and swaps them for cleaner summary information before making predictions.

problem.h2: Why patches with bad data kill forecasts
paras: Forecasting looks at a time series (a list of measurements over time) and predicts what comes next. A common trick: divide the series into small chunks called patches, process each one, and combine them. This works because each patch captures local patterns.

But real data is broken. Sensors fail (missing values), equipment drifts (the baseline shifts), rare events spike (anomalies), or random noise creeps in. When a patch contains corrupted or shifted measurements, the forecaster learns from garbage and makes wild predictions.

A naive solution: clean the patches first, but you cannot know what 'clean' looks like in the middle of a time series, and erasing data leaves gaps. Existing methods just use all patches, even the broken ones.

callout.html: Detect which patches contain low-quality data, and replace them with a reliable summary of the whole series.

steps.text: Cut time series into patches; turn each into a vector (a list of numbers).
Multiple specialist neural networks each process patches, combining their opinions.
A filter scores each patch for quality; low scores flag corruption or noise.
Compute a single trusted summary vector representing the whole series trend.
Replace flagged patches with the summary vector; forecast from the cleaner sequence.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: The paper changes which patches feed into the forecaster. Bad patches are swapped for a global summary vector (a list of numbers representing the whole series trend) before the model makes predictions.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: patch quality score
hidden.name: Patch quality score
paras: A patch quality score is a single number for each patch saying how trustworthy that chunk of measurements is. High means the chunk looks clean and normal; low means it contains noise, missing data, or abrupt shifts.

SEER estimates this score by looking at how well the expert networks agree on that patch, and by checking if the patch follows the expected pattern for that point in the series. A patch that all experts struggle with, or that violates the series trend, scores low.

heat.caption: Darker means higher patch quality; red boxes mark patches below the filter threshold.

reads.html: A patch is trustworthy if the measurements inside it look normal and consistent with the rest of the series.
Patch quality is derived from the disagreement of expert sub-networks and the deviation from expected series dynamics.

mechanism.h2: Why replacing bad patches makes forecasts honest
paras: The problem: if the forecaster trains on corrupted patches, it learns spurious patterns. A spike from noise teaches it to expect spikes; a gap from missing data teaches it to expect gaps. Then it generalizes those learned artifacts to the future, producing garbage forecasts.

SEER's move: detect patches that do not fit the series pattern, and replace them with a summary vector representing the true trend across the whole series. This summary is hard to fool because it averages over the entire history, so a single corrupted patch has tiny influence. When the forecaster retrains on the edited sequence (broken patches swapped for clean summaries), it learns only real patterns, not artifacts of corruption.

Why it works: The mixture-of-experts sub-networks give you multiple views of each patch. If all experts disagree or struggle (a sign the patch is an outlier), you flag it. The replaced vector is a global summary: much harder to fool than a single patch. The forecaster now sees a cleaner story of the series, so it learns only patterns that repeat across the entire history instead of artifacts tied to one noisy chunk, and generalization to future time steps improves because the learned rules apply more broadly.

stages.s: Raw time series with corrupted patches
Score patch quality via expert agreement and trend deviation
Filter: mark patches below quality threshold
Compute one global summary of the whole series

math.words: A patch is replaced if its quality score falls below a threshold. The score combines expert disagreement and deviation from the series baseline.
symbols: binary flag: 1 if patch i is replaced, 0 if kept
largest difference in opinion among expert networks on patch i
how far patch i's statistics sit from the series mean

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Patch 2: three experts embed it as [0.4, 0.5, 0.4]. Disagreement = max(0.4,0.5,0.4) - min = 0.1. Series baseline is [0.5, 0.5]. Deviation = sqrt((0.45-0.5)^2 + (0.45-0.5)^2) = 0.07. Total penalty = 0.1 + 0.07 = 0.17. Quality = 1/(1+0.17) = 0.89. Above threshold (0.5)? Yes, keep patch.

Patch 3: three experts encode it as [0.1, 0.8, 0.2]. Disagreement = 0.8 - 0.1 = 0.7. Series baseline [0.5, 0.5]. Deviation = sqrt((0.37-0.5)^2 + (0.37-0.5)^2) = 0.18. Total penalty = 0.7 + 0.18 = 0.88. Quality = 1/(1+0.88) = 0.53. Above 0.5? Borderline, replace.
Patch 3 replaced with global series summary [0.5, 0.5]. Now the sequence is clean.

math.note: Patches with high disagreement or large deviation are replaced; the filtering threshold is the tuning knob.

bars.h2: Forecast accuracy before and after patch replacement

charts.title: Naive: use all patches
charts.note: Corrupted training patches teach the model to expect corruption in the future, so accuracy crashes on any noisier data.

charts.title: SEER: replace bad patches
charts.note: Cleaning training patches removes spurious correlations (things the model would learn to expect from noise), so the model learns only real patterns that come from the underlying process, not from corruption. Because the learned rules ignore noise, they generalize even to new noise conditions the model has never seen.

items.html: If the quality thresholds are set too tight, you replace too many patches with summaries, losing local detail. The model might smooth out real structure in the time series.

If the corruption is systematic (the whole series is shifted, not just one patch), replacing with a global average does not help because the average baseline itself includes the shift. The summary vector carries the same corruption as the patches, so swapping them makes no difference.

items.b: Experts do not agree on anomalies.
items.html: A real anomaly (a one-time spike that is honest) will show high disagreement and might get flagged and replaced, erasing important structure from the series.

Set thresholds conservatively, so only patches with clear signs of corruption (high disagreement and deviation) are replaced. Monitor which patches are being replaced and retune if real structure vanishes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small time series dataset with known corruption: inject missing-value chunks, noise spikes, or changes in the measurement baseline into specific patches. Train SEER and a baseline forecaster on the corrupted series. On test data with and without matching corruption, measure forecast accuracy as the difference between predicted and true future values.
demo.metric_eq: robustness_gain = baseline_accuracy_clean - baseline_accuracy_corrupted) - (SEER_accuracy_clean - SEER_accuracy_corrupted); a positive gain means SEER's forecasts are hurt less by corruption.
demo.closing: The demo should show that SEER's forecast accuracy drops far less than the baseline when the test data is corrupted in the same way as the training corruption (i.e., the replacement mechanism learns to ignore the corruption pattern, not memorize it).
